title: Linguistic Nepotism: Trading-off Quality for Language Preference in Multilingual RAG
claim: Language preference can be measured by translating evidence, generating verified citation-supported reports, then tracking how citation prediction changes with document language.
layout: 4 numbered step panels, left-to-right then top-to-bottom, color-tinted backgrounds per stage
description: A four-step pipeline diagram on tinted panels. A dashed box at top-left shows the query 'How does fingerprint unlock work on phones?' with three numbered evidence documents. Step 1 (blue) translates the English document into French, Arabic and Korean via a translate icon, shown as stacked cards with language labels. Step 2 generates a reference report from the query plus citation IDs 1, 2 and 3 through a neural-net icon, giving a cited paragraph. Step 3 (top right, blue) filters statements with an LLM-as-Judge (Supported/Rejected tags) and an NLI entailment classifier. Accepted statements go into a Statement Pool, with a loop arrow labeled 'Repeat for all statements'. Step 4 (pink) shows next-token citation probability expressions Pr(...|Query, 1, 2[English/French/Arabic], 3). Circled numbers and green checkmarks guide the eye.
caption: Overview of our approach for measuring language preference. We show both synthetic data generation and measurement method. Given an English query q and its K relevant evidence documents Den, we first translate the documents into multiple languages Dfr, Dar, Dko . . . (Step 1). We then generate a reference citation-supported report r for each query using q and Den (Step 2). The report r consists of sentence-level statements si, each paired with a single citation ID ci. For each r, we retain only statements that are verified (Step 3). Language preference is detected when the next token prediction accuracy for the correct citation ID decreases as the language of the cited document is varied (Step 4).
abstract: Multilingual Retrieval-Augmented Generation (mRAG) systems enable language models to answer knowledge-intensive queries with citation-supported responses across languages. Despite their growing use, an open questions is whether the mixture of different document languages impacts generation and citation behavior in unintended ways. To investigate this, we introduce a controlled methodology using model internals to measure language preference while holding other factors such as document relevance constant. Across eight languages and six open-weight models, we find that models preferentially cite English sources when queries are in English, with this bias amplified for lower-resource languages and for documents positioned mid-context. More crucially, we find that models sometimes trade-off document relevance for language preference, indicating that citation choices are not always driven by informativeness alone. Our findings shed light on how language models leverage multilingual context and influence citation behavior.
